title: Architecture-dependent Effects of Trade-offs on Evolutionary Navigability and Epistasis
summary: The structure of the genotype-phenotype map plays a central role in determining how populations move through fitness landscapes, yet less is known about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs. Here, we study evolution on a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map in which binary genotypes are transformed through successive feed-forward layers before being evaluated by phenotype-level fitness functions. We explicitly model the phenotype to fitness transformation in order to compare an emergent trade-off fitness with a no-trade-off control. We explore different map architecture as models of more and less complex genotype-phenotype relationships by tuning the genotype length and number of layers. We find that ruggedness and navigability have a complex, architecture-dependent relationship. Landscapes with few local maxima can still have low navigability for wide and shallow maps, and navigability is high even at mean values of ruggedness for wide and deep maps. Trade-offs increase navigability in wide and shallow maps, while their effect is muted in other architectures. The effect of trade-offs on epistasis depends on evolutionary history. While trade-offs change which mutational neighborhoods are sampled by evolution, the background degree of epistatic interactions is set by map architecture. Finally, we use our framework to investigate micro-evolution of high-fitness populations and show that temporal covariance in allele-frequency changes can arise from the internal structure of a rugged genotype-phenotype map, producing signatures that resemble short-term alternating selection.

AI.tldr: This paper studies evolution on tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype maps, finding that landscape ruggedness and navigability have architecture-dependent relationships, trade-offs improve navigability mainly in wide/shallow maps, and internal map structure can produce allele-frequency covariance signatures resembling alternating selection.
AI.motivation: While the structure of genotype-phenotype maps is known to shape evolutionary dynamics, less is understood about how this structure interacts with environmental constraints and fitness trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors use a tunable multilayer genotype-phenotype map where binary genotypes pass through successive feed-forward layers before phenotype-level fitness evaluation. They explicitly model phenotype-to-fitness transformation to compare trade-off versus no-trade-off scenarios, and vary genotype length and number of layers to explore different map architectures.
AI.result: Ruggedness and navigability show architecture-dependent relationships—wide/shallow maps can have low navigability despite few local maxima, while wide/deep maps are navigable even at mean ruggedness. Trade-offs increase navigability only in wide/shallow maps. Trade-off effects on epistasis depend on evolutionary history; background epistasis is set by architecture while trade-offs alter which mutational neighborhoods are sampled. Internal map structure in rugged landscapes can generate temporal allele-frequency covariance resembling short-term alternating selection.
AI.conclusion: The internal structure of genotype-phenotype maps and their architecture fundamentally shape evolutionary dynamics, navigation, epistasis sampling, and even produce selection-like signatures from map structure alone, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling phenotype-fitness transformations beyond simple landscape models.

title: SurfSpec: Enhancing Off-Target-Agnostic Specificity by Bounding Pocket-Ligand Geometric Mismatch
summary: Lead optimization in structure-based drug design aims to improve target binding while avoiding unintended interactions with off-target pockets. However, existing affinity-driven methods do not explicitly control specificity, whereas current specificity-aware approaches commonly require prior knowledge of off-target structures. We address off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization by analyzing the geometric mismatch between a ligand and the target pocket. We provide a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets without requiring access to off-target structures. By metricizing pocket--ligand mismatch, the triangle inequality shows that reducing target--ligand mismatch improves a conservative lower bound on mismatch to a separated off-target class, which can be translated into a specificity lower bound through an empirical geometry--affinity calibration. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce SurfSpec, an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. SurfSpec alternates between linker generation toward selected target-surface patches, which provides geometric pseudo-labels, and refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior, which restores these pseudo-labels into valid ligands. On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.

AI.tldr: SurfSpec is an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that improves ligand specificity by growing molecules toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. It leverages a conservative specificity lower bound derived from geometric mismatch via triangle inequality and an empirical geometry-affinity calibration, without requiring any knowledge of off-target structures.
AI.motivation: Existing affinity-driven lead optimization methods do not control off-target specificity, while specificity-aware approaches require prior knowledge of off-target structures, which is often unavailable. The paper addresses the need for specificity-aware lead optimization that works without off-target structural information.
AI.method: SurfSpec iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. It alternates between (1) linker generation toward selected target-surface patches providing geometric pseudo-labels, and (2) refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior that restores pseudo-labels into valid ligands. The theoretical foundation uses a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets, derived by metricizing pocket-ligand mismatch and applying triangle inequality, translated into a specificity lower bound via empirical geometry-affinity calibration.
AI.result: On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.
AI.conclusion: SurfSpec demonstrates that specificity can be improved in lead optimization without any access to off-target structures, by carefully growing ligands to better fit the target pocket and thus implicitly increasing geometric separation from off-target pockets.

title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
summary: Histology images contain rich morphological information and can provide insights into pathological processes. However, deriving hypotheses relating morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by a manual image interpretation step. Here, we demonstrate that this process can be automated through interpretable deep learning. We present SCOPE, a method to interpret slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision--language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. To measure whether such explanations recover known morphology, we introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. On this benchmark, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology; decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost. Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can thus generate morphological hypotheses at scale, for expert validation.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a method that interprets slide-level histology classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision-language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank, automated morphology analysis. Evaluated on MorphoRecoveryBench (7 tasks with pathologist-curated references), it shows sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology while dense attribution performs no better than random; a decomposed pooled slide embedding achieves similar accuracy at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Deriving hypotheses linking morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by manual image interpretation of histology slides. There is a need to automate this process with interpretable deep learning methods that can recover meaningful morphological descriptions at scale.
AI.method: SCOPE interprets slide-level classifiers through pathology-specific vision-language models combined with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. It is validated on MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. Sparse and dense attribution approaches are compared against a random baseline, alongside a computationally cheaper decomposed pooled slide embedding approach.
AI.result: Dense concept attribution performs no better than a random baseline, while sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology. Decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches explanation correctness comparable to sparse attribution at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can effectively generate morphological hypotheses at scale, enabling expert-guided validation and substantially reducing the manual bottleneck in histology image analysis.

title: Advances in Machine Learning for Directed Evolution: A Five-Year Retrospective
summary: The last five-plus years have seen many protein engineering disciplines transformed by advances in machine learning (ML), but the same cannot be said for directed evolution. Reflecting on a previously co-authored perspective, I discuss why I believe this to be the case, arguing that a disconnect between the goals of machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) researchers--"identify an optimal protein"--and the goals of directed evolution more broadly--"identify a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints"--is a principal culprit. As an example, I highlight how nearly all current MLDE methods neglect to account for the cost of DNA synthesis, resulting in strategies that have limited practical applicability regardless of the underlying models' capabilities. I close by discussing recent works that are exceptions to this overarching trend, and emphasize that the last five years of efforts in ML-assisted protein engineering and the prescribed reframe of MLDE objectives need not be mutually exclusive.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper argues that machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) research has failed to transform directed evolution practice because of a fundamental goal mismatch: MLDE researchers aim to "identify an optimal protein" while directed evolution practitioners need to "identify a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints." The author highlights that most MLDE methods ignore DNA synthesis costs, limiting practical applicability, and discusses recent exceptions to this trend.
AI.motivation: While machine learning has transformed many protein engineering disciplines over the past five years, it has not similarly impacted directed evolution. The author seeks to explain this gap by reflecting on the disconnect between MLDE research goals and the practical goals of directed evolution practitioners.
AI.method: This is a perspective/opinion paper based on the author's reflective analysis of prior co-authored work, using the neglect of DNA synthesis costs in MLDE methods as a concrete case study illustrating the broader goal mismatch between optimization-focused MLDE research and resource-constrained directed evolution practice.
AI.result: The author identifies the principal cause of ML's limited impact on directed evolution: a fundamental misalignment between MLDE's optimization objective (finding the optimal protein) and directed evolution's practical objective (finding a sufficient protein within time and resource limits). Nearly all current MLDE methods fail to account for DNA synthesis costs, making them impractical regardless of model capability.
AI.conclusion: The author suggests that recent works serve as exceptions to the overarching trend, and argues that the past five years of ML-assisted protein engineering efforts and the proposed reframe of MLDE objectives are not mutually exclusive—they can be reconciled.

title: Enhancer-promoter proximity predicts transcriptional competence but not transcriptional output in the Drosophila brain
summary: How 3D genome architecture contributes to transcriptional specificity across neuronal cell types remains unclear. Here, we used multiplexed chromatin tracing to map chromatin architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain. We found that enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity was increased in transcriptionally active compared with inactive neurons. Analysis of single traces revealed the existence of distinct proximal and distal E-P states, with active neurons enriched in the proximal state. However, this relationship broke down across active neuronal subtypes, where neither E-P proximity nor chromatin accessibility predicted transcriptional output. Thus, 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent from inactive neuronal states without quantitatively specifying transcriptional output. Our findings support a model in which E-P proximity establishes a permissive structural state, while additional cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms tune transcriptional output.

AI.tldr: Using multiplexed chromatin tracing in the adult Drosophila brain, this study shows that enhancer-promoter proximity distinguishes transcriptionally active from inactive neurons, but does not quantitatively predict transcriptional output across active neuronal subtypes, supporting a model where 3D genome architecture establishes a permissive state while other regulatory mechanisms tune transcription.
AI.motivation: To understand how 3D genome architecture contributes to cell-type-specific transcriptional regulation in the brain, where the relationship between chromatin organization and transcriptional specificity across neuronal subtypes remains unclear.
AI.method: Multiplexed chromatin tracing was used to map chromatin architecture and cell identity at single-cell resolution in the adult Drosophila brain, enabling analysis of enhancer-promoter proximity in individual cells.
AI.result: E-P proximity was increased in transcriptionally active neurons compared to inactive ones, and active neurons were enriched in a proximal E-P state. However, across active neuronal subtypes, neither E-P proximity nor chromatin accessibility predicted transcriptional output.
AI.conclusion: 3D genome organization distinguishes transcriptionally competent from inactive neuronal states but does not quantitatively specify transcriptional output. E-P proximity creates a permissive structural state, with additional cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms tuning transcription levels.

title: An Integrative Computational Approach to Predict Viral Epitopes by Targeting the MHC-TCR Complexation
summary: T-cell immunity acts as a major defense system against controlling viral infections in vertebrates. During viral entry, innate immune cells degrade the viral proteins (antigens) and present them on their surface via Major Histocompatibility (MHC) proteins. T-cell receptors (TCRs) recognize these antigens/peptides presented by MHC (pMHC), initiating a T-cell mediated immune response. Despite its significance, the mechanism by which pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation remains unclear. In this study, we employed an integrative computational approach combining Bioinformatics, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, and Machine Learning (ML) to identify viral epitopes as potential vaccine candidates. We performed large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations on MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded into dendritic and T-cells, for which experimental immunogenicity data is available. One hundred fifty such systems are simulated for 1 μs each to capture the conformational and dynamical changes that underlie T-cell activation. Our ML model (DynamiT), trained on simulation-derived structural and dynamical features extracted from 2500 time points, revealed key determinants responsible for T-cell activation with an accuracy of 73.3%. Notably, we have identified the bending of the TCR transmembrane region, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region and the buried surface area at the pMHC and TCR interface as critical factors influencing immune response initiation. Our approach unravels the mechanism of T-cell mediated immune response and helps ML-guided screening of viral epitopes for vaccine development.

AI.tldr: This study uses an integrative computational approach combining bioinformatics, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and machine learning to investigate the mechanism of pMHC-TCR binding that triggers T-cell activation, and to identify viral epitopes as vaccine candidates. They simulated 150 MHC-peptide-TCR complexes for 1 μs each and trained an ML model (DynamiT) on simulation-derived features, achieving 73.3% accuracy in predicting T-cell activation. Key determinants identified include TCR transmembrane bending, TCRα constant region dynamics, and buried surface area at the pMHC-TCR interface.
AI.motivation: T-cell immunity is a major defense against viral infections, yet the mechanism by which pMHC-TCR binding triggers T-cell activation remains unclear. Understanding this mechanism is critical for developing effective vaccines targeting viral epitopes.
AI.method: An integrative computational pipeline was employed: (1) bioinformatics to identify viral epitopes, (2) large-scale all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations of 150 MHC-peptide-TCR complexes embedded in dendritic and T-cells (1 μs each), and (3) an ML model (DynamiT) trained on structural and dynamical features extracted from 2500 time points per simulation.
AI.result: The ML model achieved 73.3% accuracy in predicting T-cell activation. Three critical determinants were identified: bending of the TCR transmembrane region, major dynamic motions of the TCRα constant region, and the buried surface area at the pMHC-TCR interface.
AI.conclusion: The approach unravels the mechanism of T-cell mediated immune response and enables ML-guided screening of viral epitopes for vaccine development.

title: Coarse-Graining Agent-Based Models of Bacterial Infections
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) provide a natural framework for representing cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity in bacterial infections, but their computational cost limits their use for macroscopic tissue-scale simulations and broad parameter exploration. We derive a deterministic coarse-grained description for a class of bacterial-infection ABMs in which immune cells and extracellular bacteria diffuse, immune cells ingest nearby bacteria, and intracellular bacterial loads evolve through prescribed birth and clearance processes. The first coarse-grained model is a semidiscrete reaction--diffusion system that retains a discrete internal state for each immune-cell bacterial load while representing cell and bacterial populations by continuum concentration fields. The key technical step is the derivation of state-dependent effective ingestion rates from the microscopic ABM parameters: these rates are obtained by solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium and computing the flux of immune cells into the interaction region. We then take a continuum limit in the internal state variable, yielding a state-structured reaction--diffusion system in which intracellular dynamics appear as advection and diffusion in state space. Numerical comparisons with ensemble-averaged ABM simulations show close agreement in biologically motivated parameter regimes. The resulting framework preserves the rule-based structure of the ABM while producing PDE models that are substantially more tractable for large-scale simulation and parameter studies.

AI.tldr: The authors derive deterministic coarse-grained PDE models from agent-based models (ABMs) of bacterial infections, where immune cells and bacteria diffuse, cells ingest nearby bacteria, and intracellular bacterial loads evolve. They first obtain a semidiscrete reaction-diffusion system with discrete internal states, then take a continuum limit in the internal state variable to yield a state-structured reaction-diffusion system. Key technical contribution is deriving state-dependent effective ingestion rates from microscopic parameters via an auxiliary diffusion problem. Numerical comparisons show close agreement with ensemble-averaged ABM simulations, yielding tractable PDE models preserving ABM rule-based structure.
AI.motivation: Agent-based models of bacterial infections capture cell-level rules and spatial heterogeneity but are computationally expensive, limiting their use for large-scale tissue simulations and broad parameter exploration. The authors aim to derive computationally tractable coarse-grained descriptions that retain the essential physiology.
AI.method: The authors derive a deterministic coarse-grained model in two stages: (1) a semidiscrete reaction-diffusion system preserving discrete immune-cell bacterial load states with continuum concentration fields for cell and bacterial populations, using state-dependent effective ingestion rates derived from solving an auxiliary diffusion problem around a single bacterium; (2) a continuum limit in the internal state variable producing a state-structured reaction-diffusion system where intracellular dynamics appear as advection and diffusion in state space.
AI.result: Numerical comparisons demonstrate close agreement between the derived PDE models and ensemble-averaged ABM simulations across biologically motivated parameter regimes. The framework produces PDE models substantially more tractable for large-scale simulation and parameter studies while preserving the rule-based structure of the ABM.
AI.conclusion: The derived coarse-grained framework bridges ABMs and PDE models for bacterial infections, offering a scalable and principled way to study macroscopic tissue-scale dynamics and explore parameter spaces while retaining mechanistic fidelity to underlying cell-level rules.

title: Structural control over equilibrium silicon and oxygen isotopic fractionation: A first-principles density-functional theory study
summary: Isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in selected silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) have been calculated using first-principles methods. Good agreement between theory and experiment is obtained in the case of oxygen. In the case of silicon, agreement and differences with existing estimates of equilibrium fractionation factors are discussed. The relationships between silicon fractionation factors and oxygen fractionation factors, silicate polymerization degree and chemical composition is studied. The previously stated relationship with the polymerization degree of the mineral is not confirmed. Nevertheless, our calculation suggests that silicon fractionation depends on the cationic content of the mineral, in a way similar to oxygen.  Oxygen fractionation properties could thus provide some insights on silicon fractionation behavior.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations of oxygen and silicon isotopic fractionation factors in five silicates (quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, kaolinite) show good agreement with experiments for oxygen, while silicon fractionation correlates with cationic content rather than polymerization degree.
AI.motivation: To determine equilibrium isotopic fractionation factors for oxygen and silicon in silicates using first-principles methods, and to investigate what controls silicon fractionation behavior—specifically testing the previously proposed relationship with silicate polymerization degree.
AI.method: First-principles (ab initio) calculations of isotopic reduced partition function ratios for oxygen and silicon in quartz, enstatite, forsterite, lizardite, and kaolinite, followed by comparison with experimental data and analysis of correlations with structural and compositional parameters.
AI.result: Oxygen fractionation factors agree well with experiments. The previously proposed relationship between silicon fractionation and polymerization degree is not confirmed. Instead, silicon fractionation appears to depend on the cationic content of the mineral, analogous to oxygen behavior.
AI.conclusion: Silicon isotopic fractionation in silicates is controlled by cationic composition rather than polymerization degree, and oxygen fractionation properties can serve as a proxy for predicting silicon fractionation behavior.

title: The Identification of Biological Stains at Crime Scenes: A Promising Role for Proteomics and Machine Learning
summary: Forensic body fluid identification is crucial for reconstructing crime scene events. While DNA analysis provides individualization, it lacks information about the fluid's origin. We developed and evaluated three complementary proteomic approaches using LC-HRMS/MS to identify blood, saliva, semen, urine, and vaginal fluid, including complex mixtures. The first method utilized fluid-specific peptide biomarkers, achieving high accuracy for pure fluids. The second employed peptide abundance ratios, demonstrating effectiveness in body fluid mixtures. The third, a machine learning model using Classifier Chain Random Forest, achieved 100% accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures. Our results revealed the complementarity of different tests, with the peptide-specific biomarker and machine-learning approaches being the most robust. This study demonstrates the potential of proteomics for comprehensive body fluid identification, offering valuable tools for forensic investigations.

AI.tldr: This study develops and evaluates three complementary proteomic approaches (fluid-specific peptide biomarkers, peptide abundance ratios, and a Classifier Chain Random Forest machine learning model) using LC-HRMS/MS to identify five body fluids (blood, saliva, semen, urine, vaginal fluid) including complex mixtures, demonstrating high accuracy for pure fluids and promising results for mixtures.
AI.motivation: Forensic body fluid identification is essential for crime scene reconstruction, but traditional DNA analysis only provides individualization without revealing the fluid's origin, creating a gap that needs to be filled.
AI.method: Three complementary proteomic approaches were developed and evaluated using LC-HRMS/MS: (1) fluid-specific peptide biomarkers for pure fluid identification, (2) peptide abundance ratios for body fluid mixtures, and (3) a machine learning model using Classifier Chain Random Forest.
AI.result: The peptide-specific biomarker approach achieved high accuracy for pure fluids, the abundance ratio method was effective for mixtures, and the machine learning model achieved 100% accuracy on pure fluids with promising results on mixtures. The biomarker and ML approaches were found to be the most robust and complementary.
AI.conclusion: Proteomics offers comprehensive body fluid identification capabilities and provides valuable tools for forensic investigations, addressing the limitation of DNA analysis in determining fluid origin.

title: Modeling Tissue Detachment and Rupture Using an Extended Vertex Model with T2-inverse Transitions
summary: The vertex model is widely used to describe the mechanics of epithelial tissues, but its conventional formulation assumes that all cells remain tightly packed and always share edges with their neighbors, making it difficult to represent local detachment or gap formation. Here, we propose a minimal extension of the vertex model that enables cell detachment by introducing a new topological transformation, T2-inverse, which acts as the inverse of the classical T2 transition. When the imbalance of forces acting on a vertex, quantified by a tension metric $T$, exceeds a threshold, the T2-inverse splits the vertex into multiple vertices and creates a closed polygon that is incorporated as a pseudo-cell. This operation allows the model to represent the emergence and propagation of local detachment events. Using this framework, we simulate the stretching of a cell sheet and show that force-induced local detachments can accumulate to produce macroscopic tissue rupture. These results demonstrate that the proposed model extends the capability of the vertex model to describe tissue-level breakdown processes, including detachment and tearing, and provides a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a minimal extension to the vertex model of epithelial tissues by introducing a new topological transformation called T2-inverse, which enables cell detachment and gap formation. When a tension metric exceeds a threshold, the T2-inverse splits vertices and creates pseudo-cells, allowing the simulation of local detachment events that can accumulate into macroscopic tissue rupture under stretching.
AI.motivation: The conventional vertex model assumes cells remain tightly packed and always share edges with neighbors, making it incapable of representing local detachment or gap formation—phenomena critical to processes like tissue tearing and breakdown.
AI.method: The paper extends the vertex model by introducing a T2-inverse topological transformation that acts as the inverse of the classical T2 transition. When the tension metric T at a vertex exceeds a threshold, the vertex splits into multiple vertices and a closed polygon is created and incorporated as a pseudo-cell, enabling representation of detachment events.
AI.result: Simulations of cell sheet stretching show that force-induced local detachments can accumulate to produce macroscopic tissue rupture, demonstrating the model's capability to describe tissue-level breakdown processes including detachment and tearing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model extends the vertex model's capability to describe tissue-level breakdown processes, providing a foundation for studying a broader class of epithelial mechanical phenomena such as detachment and tearing.

title: High-Order Triadic Functional Connectivity in the Brain and Beyond
summary: Here, we report high-order functional network connectivity as a promising way for studying the brain connectome. Traditional functional connectivity approaches capture only pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking complex multivariate dependencies that underlie cognition and behavior. First, we demonstrated that high-order interactions capture more information and can distinguish between resting-state and task-state brain activity. Second, we introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions, which are statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions, and apply it to large-scale functional brain networks. The resulting triadic networks revealed distinct community patterns that complement those observed in traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses and simultaneously capture additional connection information. Despite the potential combinatorial explosion of triadic configurations, the networks exhibited constrained and hierarchical structures that allowed computation and interpretation. These findings position triadic connectivity as a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, while also highlighting key biological and technical challenges that require careful consideration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces high-order functional network connectivity, specifically triadic (three-way) interactions between brain regions, as a new framework for studying the brain connectome. Using a matrix-based entropy-functional method on large-scale functional brain networks, the authors show that triadic connectivity captures more information than traditional pairwise methods, distinguishes between resting-state and task-state activity, and reveals complementary community structures—while noting the manageable computational and interpretational constraints of these higher-order networks.
AI.motivation: Traditional functional connectivity methods only capture pairwise relationships between brain regions, overlooking the complex multivariate dependencies that underlie cognition and behavior. The authors seek a more comprehensive framework for understanding brain network organization.
AI.method: The authors introduce a matrix-based entropy-functional method for estimating triadic interactions—statistical dependencies among triplets of brain regions—and apply this approach to large-scale functional brain networks to construct high-order connectivity networks.
AI.result: High-order interactions capture more information and can distinguish between resting-state and task-state brain activity. The resulting triadic networks revealed distinct community patterns that complement traditional pairwise functional connectivity analyses while capturing additional connection information. Despite combinatorial explosion concerns, the networks exhibited constrained and hierarchical structures that remained computationally tractable and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Triadic connectivity represents a promising next-step functional connectivity framework for probing brain network organization and high-order neural interactions, though key biological and technical challenges remain that require careful consideration.

title: Axonal delay dispersion decides whether a neuron detects an event or a sequence, and predicts cortical column diameter
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures, under preparation for PLOS Computational Biology
summary: Cortical neurons fire sparsely -- often fewer than one spike per sensory window -- making rate coding insufficient and temporal coding a necessity. That conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony is long established. What governs which class of temporal feature a neuron detects -- one volley of coincident input, or two in a particular order -- has not been examined. We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, via calcium plateau thresholds, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. In simulations of an integrator-neuron model we report three results. First, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity: at narrow dispersion sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval with a slope statistically indistinguishable from one. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes, not only a regulator of speed. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of about a millisecond, with slowing better tolerated than speeding. Third, that millisecond window and horizontal conduction velocity together predict cortical column diameter, and the two areas with direct measurements fall where the relation puts them. One anatomically measurable parameter thus sets what a neuron detects and the limits of what it can represent.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "delay-signature framework" where axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch act as a physical key that determines which temporal features a neuron detects. Using simulations, they show that the dispersion of delay sets is the key scalar that moves a neuron population from event detection to order-selective sequence detection, with this transition emerging from random delays and connectivity. The framework also reveals that dispersion bounds the codable interval, sets timing tolerances (~1ms), and predicts cortical column diameter from conduction velocity, mapping computational distinctions onto anatomical differences like myelination.
AI.motivation: Cortical neurons fire sparsely, making rate coding insufficient and temporal coding necessary. While it's known that conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony, what determines which class of temporal feature a neuron detects (single coincident volley vs. ordered sequence of two) has not been examined. The paper addresses this gap by proposing that the physical delay structure itself governs the computation.
AI.method: The authors propose a delay-signature framework where axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch constitute a physical key. Only input sequences with spike-time differences that the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection via calcium plateau thresholds converts synchrony into all-or-none output. They simulate an integrator-neuron model to examine how the dispersion of delay sets affects detection properties.
AI.result: Three key results emerge: (1) Delay dispersion moves populations from event detection to order-selective sequence detection with an emergent transition—sequence detectors don't exist at narrow dispersion, and the crossover dispersion tracks inter-event interval with slope statistically indistinguishable from one; (2) Dispersion bounds the longest codable interval and sets ~1ms absolute timing tolerance, with slowing tolerated better than speeding; (3) The millisecond window and horizontal conduction velocity together predict cortical column diameter, matching the two areas with direct measurements.
AI.conclusion: One anatomically measurable parameter—delay dispersion—determines both what a neuron detects (event vs. ordered sequence) and the representational limits of that detection. The framework maps a computational distinction onto myelination (anatomical), making myelination a functional switch on neuronal computation, not just a speed regulator.

title: Enumerating Chemical Structures, Stereoisomers, and Stereogenic Units with Analytic Combinatorics
comment: Submitted to J. Math. Chem. 27 pages, 7 figures
summary: The enumeration of chemical structures traditionally relies on graph- and group-theoretic techniques, including Pólya theory, in order to account for stereochemical symmetries. These methods require bespoke derivations and methods for each molecular family of interest, and quickly become very intricate for nontrivial classes. In this work, we demonstrate that analytic combinatorics provides a unifying, highly extensible, and relatively simple framework for enumeration problems. Using the symbolic method, we show that classical counting problems, such as the enumeration of acyclic alkanes and other hydrocarbon families, can be naturally solved via concise combinatorial specifications of the class of interest. We first demonstrate the simplicity of this approach by replicating existing results in this framework, requiring significantly less work than previously necessary, and then extend these ideas to more complex problems, counting broader classes of molecules accounting for both tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, counting the distribution of stereogenic units, and enumerating achiral and meso compounds. All results are made reproducible through CombOL, our open-source software package which automates the translation of combinatorial specifications into generating functions using the symbolic method, and performs both univariate and multivariate enumeration.

AI.tldr: This paper presents analytic combinatorics as a unifying framework for enumerating chemical structures, using the symbolic method to solve classical counting problems (e.g., acyclic alkanes and hydrocarbons) with far less effort than traditional graph/group-theoretic approaches, and extending to more complex problems including tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso compounds—all made reproducible via their open-source software CombOL.
AI.motivation: Traditional enumeration of chemical structures relies on graph- and group-theoretic methods (e.g., Pólya theory) that require bespoke derivations for each molecular family and become very intricate for nontrivial classes. The authors seek a simpler, more unifying, and extensible framework for these enumeration problems.
AI.method: The authors apply analytic combinatorics using the symbolic method, constructing concise combinatorial specifications of molecular classes, which are automatically translated into generating functions—both univariate and multivariate—for enumeration. They implement this in an open-source software package called CombOL.
AI.result: The approach successfully replicates existing results (e.g., acyclic alkane enumeration) with significantly less work than previously needed, and extends to more complex problems: counting broader molecular classes with tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, counting distributions of stereogenic units, and enumerating achiral and meso compounds.
AI.conclusion: Analytic combinatorics via the symbolic method offers a simple, unifying, and highly extensible framework for chemical enumeration problems, outperforming traditional methods in simplicity while covering a broader range of complex problems, with CombOL ensuring reproducibility.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: A unified computational framework for tensor-based morphometry that combines surface modeling, diffusion smoothing via Laplace-Beltrami operator estimation, and statistical analysis to localize cortical surface shape differences (area and curvature) between clinical groups, demonstrated on longitudinal gray matter growth and loss in children.
AI.motivation: Cortical surface shape differences (local area and curvature) between clinical groups are non-uniform across the brain, and existing methods lack a coherent framework to localize these regional structural differences from MRI data while dealing with noise.
AI.method: The approach integrates three components in a unified mathematical framework: (1) surface modeling of the 2D convoluted cortical sheet, (2) diffusion smoothing based on explicit estimation of the Laplace-Beltrami operator to increase signal-to-noise ratio, and (3) statistical analysis comparing surface metrics (local area and curvature) between clinical groups.
AI.result: The method successfully localizes cortical regions of gray matter tissue growth and loss in longitudinally collected brain images from a group of children, demonstrating its applicability in detecting regional structural differences.
AI.conclusion: The unified tensor-based surface morphometry approach provides a coherent framework to localize the most rapid structural differences across the cortex by combining surface modeling, Laplace-Beltrami-based diffusion smoothing, and statistical analysis.

title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
summary: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes understanding LLM adoption through a viral/spreading dynamics framework, modeling transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users. It demonstrates that social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can produce tipping points and technological lock-in, potentially leading to runaway dynamics toward persistent dependence with cognitive competence losses, while also identifying conditions for "cognitive immunization."
AI.motivation: LLMs are rapidly integrating into society and reshaping information production and use, yet their population-level diffusion dynamics and long-term cognitive consequences remain poorly understood. The authors aim to provide a framework for understanding how LLM adoption spreads and can become entrenched.
AI.method: The authors use a viral analogy to model LLM diffusion, formalizing state transitions among three user types (uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent). The model incorporates social transmission, recovery processes, and collective reinforcement to analyze population-level dynamics and identify tipping point behavior.
AI.result: The model reveals nonlinear dynamics including tipping points and technological lock-in. Once a critical adoption threshold is crossed, small increases can trigger abrupt, runaway population-level shifts toward persistent dependence accompanied by losses in cognitive competence. The framework also identifies conditions for cognitive immunization through reducing transmission and enhancing reversibility.
AI.conclusion: LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with significant implications for cognitive autonomy, and understanding these dynamics is critical for anticipating and potentially mitigating undesirable runaway adoption outcomes.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimpleDesign is a single-stage, end-to-end multi-modal protein design model trained directly in data space, using a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture with modality-specific processing and global self-attention to co-design sequences and structures.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal protein generative models rely on a multi-stage training process (first autoencoder tokenization, then latent-space generative modeling). The authors hypothesize this multi-stage training is unnecessary for performant co-design models.
AI.method: SimpleDesign is trained with a single-stage end-to-end objective combining discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. It uses a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture allowing modality-specific processing while maintaining global self-attention over both modalities. Trained on over 2M sequence-structure pairs.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A single-stage end-to-end training approach in data space can effectively model the multi-modal relationship between protein sequences and structures, challenging the necessity of multi-stage latent-space pipelines.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent species distribution modelling framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) neural network trained end-to-end via backpropagation. Applied to Desert Locust habitat mapping using 50-day environmental time series, RNN Maxent outperforms standard Maxent (ROC AUC 0.862 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 vs. 0.590).
AI.motivation: Standard Maxent relies on linear combinations of hand-chosen feature transforms, which cannot capture nonlinear, temporal relationships in ecological monitoring data. When applied to time-series covariates (e.g., precipitation, soil moisture, vegetation indices), standard implementations flatten the data into independent features, discarding the sequential structure that carries critical signal for modelling species like the Desert Locust whose breeding is coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions.
AI.method: RNN Maxent replaces the fixed feature dictionary in Maxent with a GRU-based neural network trained end-to-end via backpropagation. It preserves Maxent's presence-only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration—only the nonlinearity is learned from data. The model was applied to Desert Locust habitat mapping using 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, with a 7-day gap between covariates and presence records for forecasting behavior.
AI.result: RNN Maxent outperforms standard Maxent across evaluation metrics: ROC AUC improves from 0.792 to 0.862 (std 0.036), and F1 improves from 0.590 to 0.671 (std 0.056).
AI.conclusion: Learning nonlinearity from temporal data rather than fixing it in advance enables better capture of the sequential environmental signals important for Desert Locust habitat prediction, suggesting RNN-based extensions of Maxent are a promising direction for SDM with time-series covariates.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a simple deterministic artificial agent with an affective system (experiencing uncertainty about intrinsic needs relative to environmental resources) can display hedonic place preference behavior—arguably a subjective form of information processing—without any conscious experience or free will, challenging assumptions that such behavior indicates feelings.
AI.motivation: Scientists often infer that creatures displaying hedonic place preference behavior toward non-nutritive pleasure substances (e.g., cocaine, morphine) must experience feelings, since such attraction seems inexplicable by unconscious instinct. The authors aim to question this assumption by demonstrating that similar behavior can arise in a purely deterministic artificial system.
AI.method: The authors construct a simple artificial agent that instantiates key attributes of an affective system: it engages in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources, processing information in an apparently subjective manner while remaining entirely deterministic.
AI.result: The artificial agent successfully displays hedonic place preference behavior through a deterministic, apparently subjective form of information processing, without possessing consciousness or free will.
AI.conclusion: The findings have implications for understanding the physical basis of consciousness and free will: if deterministic agents can produce behavior typically associated with subjective feelings, then hedonic place preference behavior may not be reliable evidence for conscious experience, prompting reconsideration of what behavioral markers truly indicate phenomenal consciousness.

title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
summary: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs), and ask whether this failure mode can be addressed by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective. Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the intervention in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF reaches 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. These results identify RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs)—complex-valued temporal filters derived from an energy model that are a special case of diagonal state-space models—and proposes a parameter-free prospective-input correction to address depth-dependent top-down error attenuation and bottom-up signal delays in deep recurrent networks. Prospective variants match or outperform controls across RQF, S5, and ORGaNIC models under full BPTT and spatial-only backpropagation, achieving strong results on raw-audio Speech Commands and Path-X.
AI.motivation: Deep stacks of continuous-time recurrent networks face a fundamental tension: temporal integration provides memory but introduces delays in bottom-up signal propagation and attenuates top-down error signals. The authors ask whether making each layer's bottom-up input "prospective" (predictive of its future value) can resolve this failure mode.
AI.method: The authors derive RQF dynamics from an energy model, showing each RQF acts as a band-pass filter with learnable tuning frequency and bandwidth. They apply a parameter-free two-tap prospective update to bottom-up inputs, leaving the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged, and generalize this correction to diagonal SSMs. They evaluate prospective variants against non-prospective controls using both full BPTT and spatial-only backpropagation across RQF, S5, and ORGaNIC models.
AI.result: Prospective variants match or outperform non-prospective controls in every model and configuration under full BPTT. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with only 31.9k parameters, and a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task.
AI.conclusion: RQFs are identified as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate, and prospective-input coding serves as an effective input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks, mitigating depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated.
